entry.evidence: It is therefore surprising that locally patches of sand or even pebbly sand occur

sequences.source_document: Published paper PDF with publisher XML text

steps.action: The authors draw on decades of soil-survey data and ditch-wall maps covering more than 1500 km in the reclaimed polders, made by other groups, alongside their own fieldwork.
steps.quote: In addition to our own fieldwork, we have taken advantage of the above-mentioned studies for the present contribution.

steps.action: The silty Almere deposits are characterised as seven units by grain size, carbonate and organic content, taken from the authors' earlier work (Table 1, Fig. 3).
steps.quote: Units of the Almere deposits and their main characteristics (modified after Van Loon and Wiggers, 1975a,c).

steps.action: Isolated patches of sand and pebbly sand within the clayey-silt lagoonal deposits are reported as surprising.
steps.quote: It is therefore surprising that locally patches of sand or even pebbly sand occur

steps.action: A change in the source area or transport route is excluded, because the patches are isolated, not interconnected and lack lateral grain-size gradation; the authors infer a local cause.
steps.quote: this cannot be explained by a temporary change in the source area or a change in the transport route of these sediments.

steps.action: Three types of sand body (Tollebeek, Nagele, Kuinre) are distinguished, mainly by grain-size distribution.
steps.quote: Three different types of sand bodies have been found. They differ primarily in their grain-size distribution.

steps.action: The pebble and heavy-mineral composition of the coarse Tollebeek sands is matched to the Saalian glacial diamictons that form highs such as Urk and Schokland.
steps.quote: The composition of these pebbles and of the heavy minerals indicates that they must have been derived from glacial diamictons

steps.action: An abrasion remnant of Scandinavian boulders, cobbles and pebbles on the diamicton near Urk is presented as the trace of erosion of the till high.
steps.quote: The diamictons (assigned to the Drenthe Formation) have certainly been eroded, as is proven by the presence of an abraded area

steps.action: The rival reading that the Tollebeek sands are in-situ Drenthe till is excluded by their sedimentary structures and Holocene lagoonal and marine fossils.
steps.quote: They cannot be confused with the Drenthe Formation (although they have the same composition)

steps.action: A ditch exposure shows the Kuinre sands lying on a wave-eroded Weichselian coversand ridge, beneath the Almere deposits.
steps.quote: And, indeed, erosion took place (Fig. 11), during both the lagoonal and the subsequent more marine phase.

steps.action: The Kuinre sands are told apart from the Tollebeek sands (no coarse grains) and from the Nagele sands (poorer sorting).
steps.quote: They differ from the Nagele deposits because they are much less well sorted.

steps.action: The good sorting of the Nagele sands (mostly 105-420 µm) is matched to aeolian Weichselian river dunes of the Kreftenheye Formation that reached the lagoon bottom.
steps.quote: Because the river dunes had formed due to aeolian activity, they are well sorted, and consequently also the Nagele deposits are well sorted

steps.action: Two stratigraphic sub-units of the Nagele sands, one lagoonal and one marine, are taken from the authors' earlier work and read as slow, interrupted dune erosion.
steps.quote: According to Van Loon and Wiggers (1977), who proposed to make these sands a formal stratigraphic unit

steps.action: The origin of the sands, and the reason there are three types, is posed as the question.
steps.quote: This raises the question of how these sands came into being, and why three different types of sandy patches can be distinguished.

steps.action: Supply from the Wadden Sea and supply from the rivers and streams are set as extrabasinal rivals to local abrasion of the Pleistocene highs.
steps.quote: only two possible extrabasinal sediment sources are present: the Wadden Sea and the river/streams.

steps.action: Wadden Sea supply is excluded: that sea has little coarse sand, its sand was trapped in deltas near the present dam, and no transport route is visible.
steps.quote: the distribution of the sandy patches cannot be explained by supply of sand from the Wadden Sea.

steps.action: River supply is excluded, because river sand stays near the river mouths and differs in mineralogy from the lagoonal sands.
steps.quote: the mineralogical composition of the river sediments differs significantly from those of the lagoonal sands.

steps.action: Radiocarbon dating of the reworked peat is set aside; the sands are dated by bracketing them with units dated from cargo in embedded shipwrecks, giving ages after about 1200 A.D.
steps.quote: The datings prove that both the sediments below and above the sands date from a time span that started around 1200 A.D.

steps.action: A spatial association of the sand patches with nearby Pleistocene highs (tills, coversand ridges, river dunes) is reported, with downcurrent tails such as the 'tail of Urk'.
steps.quote: In many cases a spatial relationship is established between the Holocene sands with nearby Pleistocene ‘highs’

steps.action: Where no nearby high exists, the authors add the auxiliary that small source bodies were eroded away completely, and link sand to source by grain size, sorting and heavy minerals.
steps.quote: some of the Pleistocene sand bodies that served as a source may have been eroded completely

steps.action: After reclamation, differential compaction made the sand bodies show as slightly higher ground, still visible as undulations in roads.
steps.quote: the sand bodies underwent much less compaction, so that they became initially visible in the years after reclamation

steps.action: Comparable sand patches are reported in the other polders, with a Nagele-type sand on a river dune illustrated in Zuidelijk Flevoland; the western lake remains unknown.
steps.quote: Comparable sand patches occur in the other reclaimed polders (Oostelijk Flevoland en Zuidelijk Flevoland).

steps.action: The claim is kept that wave abrasion of Pleistocene highs produced the sand patches, so the Pleistocene palaeotopography controlled Holocene lagoonal sedimentation (schematic model, Fig. 17).
steps.quote: the palaeogeography of the local Pleistocene in the area with its slightly irregular topography controlled the sedimentary pattern in the Holocene lagoon

tree.answer: Yes: isolated sand patches within a silty Holocene lagoonal deposit
The sands are seen in ditch walls; their source and process are known only from traces
Explain the origin of the sands and why there are three types
Wadden Sea supply, river supply, change in source or transport route, and local abrasion of Pleistocene highs
Rivals differ in predicted grain size, mineralogy, transport route and spatial distribution
Conditions found in past traces, not set

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Partly: many patches, three source types, comparable patches in other polders
Weakly: only a qualitative statement that the pattern recurs in other polders
Local abrasion of Pleistocene highs kept as best explanation; extrabasinal sources excluded
Two anonymous reviewers are acknowledged, but no review file was supplied

end.claim: The sandy patches in the silty Holocene lagoonal deposits of the Noordoostpolder formed by wave abrasion of local Pleistocene highs (tills, coversand ridges, river dunes), so the Pleistocene palaeotopography controlled the Holocene sedimentary pattern.

decisive_move.sentence: Matching each sand type's composition (pebbles and heavy minerals, sorting, grain size) to a specific kind of Pleistocene high is what ties the patches to local sources rather than extrabasinal supply.

gates.evidence: The ditch mapping and soil surveys were made for agricultural soil classification, not to test a hypothesis (p. 567). The extrabasinal rivals could in principle have matched the grain size and mineralogy of the sands, and they are rejected on that basis (p. 577). However, the river mineralogy is asserted, not shown, and the absence of a nearby high is absorbed by an auxiliary assumption (pp. 579-580). Nothing was fixed before the data.

imports.item: Dating of sediment units from cargo found in embedded shipwrecks
Air photograph of the island of Urk (Nederlands Instituut voor Militaire Historie)
Soil-survey grain-size, salinity and organic-content data and ditch-wall maps of the reclaimed polders

limits: The XML file supplied contains only the abstract, figure captions and the Table 1 caption, so body steps cite printed journal pages. The paper presents no new quantitative data: no grain-size, heavy-mineral or rounding analyses are tabulated for the sands; Table 1 and the Nagele sub-units come from the authors' 1970s work. Inference: the core explanation (abrasion as a sand source) was already published by Van Loon and Wiggers (1976a), so this paper largely re-presents and synthesises earlier work rather than testing it anew. No map of patches against highs is given, and the claim that 'almost all' patches sit near highs is unquantified. Sampling, field methods and the extent of the authors' own new fieldwork are not described. The mineralogical difference from river sands is asserted without data. Where no high is found, the explanation is protected by assuming complete erosion of small sources, which weakens falsifiability. The dating sub-claim (sands younger than about 1200 A.D.) is an estimate taken from cited archaeological dating (Wiggers 1955), without stated resolution for the sands themselves. The generalisation to the other polders is stated, not documented. The acknowledgement mentions two anonymous reviewers, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: Weerts et al. (2000), current lithostratigraphic nomenclature of The Netherlands
disagreements.support: The authors argue the sand bodies formed in a brackish lagoon and so should not be lumped into the marine Naaldwijk Formation; they cite Van Loon (1981), who treated them as members of the Groningen Formation.
disagreements.quote: does not consider these exceptional sand bodies at all, and includes them in the marine Naaldwijk Formation, even though they were formed in a brackish [...]

disagreements.target: Palaeogeographical interpretations that explain local grain-size anomalies only by changes in sediment supply
disagreements.support: The Noordoostpolder case shows that local erosion of an older substratum can produce such anomalies.
disagreements.quote: should not only consider facies changes due to changes in the sediment supply, but should also consider local erosion

alternatives_considered.chosen: Local abrasion of Pleistocene highs as the sand source
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Supply from the Wadden Sea; supply from the River IJssel and smaller streams; a temporary change in source area or transport route
alternatives_considered.reason: Wadden Sea sand is fine and was trapped in deltas, with no transport route visible; river sand differs in mineralogy and stays near the river mouths; the patches are isolated with no lateral gradation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Archaeological dating from shipwreck cargo, applied through the dated Almere units
alternatives_considered.alternatives: C-14 dating of peat in the deposits
alternatives_considered.reason: The peat is reworked and cannot be used for C-14 dating

alternatives_considered.chosen: A schematic sketch with informal unit names (e.g., 'Almere deposits')
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Formal stratigraphic schemes (Groningen, Westland and Naaldwijk formations)
alternatives_considered.reason: Changing and somewhat confusing stratigraphical names
